Mountains (Biblical)
MOUN-tinz
noun
Hebrew har (H2022), Greek oros (G3735) — high places in Scripture associated with the appearance of God to His people; covenant-mountains (Sinai, Zion, Moriah, Hermon, Tabor, Carmel, Olives) form a typological geography of redemption history.

📖 Biblical Definition

Mountains in biblical theology are theophany-points — the high places where God reveals Himself, calls covenants, performs miracles, and pivots the story of redemption. The biblical canon is anchored to specific mountains: SINAI (Exod 19) where God gave the Law; MORIAH (Gen 22; 2 Chr 3:1) where Abraham bound Isaac AND where Solomon built the temple; ZION (Ps 2; 48; 132) where God set His King; HOREB (1 Kings 19) where Elijah encountered the still small voice; CARMEL (1 Kings 18) where Elijah called down fire on the prophets of Baal; HERMON or TABOR (Matt 17:1-8; 2 Pet 1:16-18) where Christ was transfigured; OLIVES (Zech 14:4; Acts 1:11-12) where Christ ascended and from which He will return; CALVARY/GOLGOTHA (Matt 27:33) — a hill not technically a mountain but functionally the climax of the redemption-mountain typology; and the eschatological MOUNT ZION (Heb 12:22 — "ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God"). The mountain pattern reaches its climax in Revelation 21:10 where John is carried "in the spirit to a great and high mountain" to see the New Jerusalem descending. Mountains in Scripture are not just topography; they are the visible markers of covenant moments — the high places where the divine and human realms most palpably meet. "Send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill" (Ps 43:3). The mountain spirituality is upward; God meets His people on the heights, and the saints lift up their eyes "unto the hills, from whence cometh my help" (Ps 121:1). At the end of all things, God Himself becomes the mountain: "the mountain of the LORD's house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it" (Isa 2:2; Mic 4:1).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

High places in biblical geography that mark theophany — Sinai (Law), Moriah (binding/temple), Zion (Kingdom), Olives (Ascension), Calvary (Cross), and the eschatological Mt. Zion of Hebrews 12.

expand to see more

MOUNTAINS, noun, plural. High elevations of the earth's surface; in Scripture the locations of theophany, covenant-giving, miracle, and pivotal redemption-history events.

Key biblical mountains: Sinai (Law); Moriah (Abraham's offering; Solomon's temple); Zion (David's throne; God's holy hill); Horeb (Elijah's still small voice); Carmel (Elijah vs. Baal); Hermon or Tabor (Transfiguration); Olives (Ascension; Second Coming); Calvary (Crucifixion); the eschatological Mt. Zion (Heb 12:22).

📖 Key Scripture

Isaiah 2:2 — "And it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the LORD's house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it."

Hebrews 12:22 — "But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels."

Psalm 121:1 — "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help."

Matthew 17:1-2 — "And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Mountains are corrupted when the theological geography of biblical mountains is dissolved into mere setting (any mountain will do), or when the eschatological Mt. Zion of Hebrews 12 is replaced with a flat-earth equality of all places before God.

expand to see more

Topography-only reading. Modernist commentary often treats biblical mountains as mere setting — Sinai is just where Moses happened to be when God spoke, Zion is just where David happened to settle, Calvary is just where the Romans happened to crucify. But the canonical text is far more theologically specific: SAME mountain at Moriah for Abraham's offering AND for Solomon's temple AND for Christ's crucifixion (Calvary is on or near Moriah). The OT and NT mountain geography forms a unified theological map; God's redemption is anchored to specific high places.

Eschatological-mountain dissolution. Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts Mount Sinai (where Israel could not approach without dying) with Mount Zion (where Christians have already come). The mountain reality is being progressively revealed: Sinai was the old-covenant mountain of unapproachable holiness; Mt. Zion is the new-covenant mountain of approached holiness through Christ. To strip the mountain typology and replace it with vague "God is everywhere equally" abstractions loses the canonical logic that God meets His people at specific, named, geographic places — and that the climactic mountain is the heavenly Mt. Zion where the throne sits.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew har (H2022), Greek oros (G3735) — mountain; the theophany-points of biblical geography.

expand to see more

Hebrew har (H2022) — mountain; appears 500+ times in Hebrew Scripture, often in covenant-mountain contexts

Greek oros (G3735) — mountain; used for the Mount of Olives, the Mount of Transfiguration, the eschatological Mt. Zion

Key canonical mountains: Sinai (Law), Moriah (binding/temple), Zion (Kingdom), Olives (Ascension), Calvary (Cross)

Eschatological climax: the mountain of the LORD's house exalted above all mountains (Isa 2:2; Mic 4:1); heavenly Mt. Zion (Heb 12:22)
